title: A microscopic coating
scenario: A fictional coating contains 3.2 × 10⁹ particles. Each has mass 7.5 × 10⁻¹⁴ g. Only 80% of the supplied material reaches the surface.

parts.prompt: Find the deposited mass in g.
parts.hint: Multiply coefficients and add exponents.

parts.prompt: Find the mass that must be supplied, in g.
parts.hint: The deposit is 0.80 of the supplied mass.

reason: Explain why multiplying the deposit by 1.20 would not reverse the 20% loss.
discussion: The loss is a percentage of the supplied mass, not of the deposit. Multiplying by 1.20 would supply only 2.88 × 10⁻⁴ g and deposit 2.304 × 10⁻⁴ g.

title: Recover a saving plan
scenario: Weekly deposits form an arithmetic sequence. The fifth deposit is 38 and the twelfth is 73.

parts.prompt: Find the first deposit.
parts.hint: Find the common difference using the seven-step gap.

parts.prompt: Find the least number of weeks needed for total deposits to reach 1000.
parts.hint: Solve the sum inequality, then check neighbouring integers.
parts.working: Sₙ = n(5n+31)/2. S₁₇ = 986 and S₁₈ = 1089, so 18 weeks.

reason: Why must the continuous solution be rounded up here?
discussion: Deposits occur at whole weeks. A fractional week has not earned the next deposit. Check the adjacent totals rather than rounding to the nearest integer.

title: Finite geometric budget
scenario: A display uses 120 lamps in its first row and 20% more in each successive row. Treat lamp counts as a continuous planning model until the final design.

parts.prompt: Find the model total for the first 6 rows.
parts.hint: Use a finite geometric sum.

parts.prompt: Find the largest whole number of rows whose model total is at most 2000.
parts.hint: Compare the totals for consecutive row counts.

reason: Explain why the actual lamp order may differ from this model.
discussion: Rows require integer counts. Rounding each row, or repeatedly rounding a recurrence, changes the total; state and apply a rounding policy before ordering.

title: Nominal gain versus purchasing power
scenario: An investment of 5000 earns 6% nominal annual interest compounded monthly for 4 years. Annual inflation is 2.5%; ignore fees and tax.

parts.prompt: Find the nominal final balance.
parts.hint: Monthly interest is 0.06/12.

parts.prompt: Find its final purchasing power in starting-year money.
parts.hint: Deflate the final balance over all four years.
parts.working: Divide the nominal balance by 1.025⁴, giving approximately 5755.00.

reason: Can the annual real return be found exactly by subtracting 2.5 from 6?
discussion: No. First obtain the effective annual nominal growth factor 1.005¹²; divide by 1.025 and subtract 1. Simple subtraction is only an approximation.

title: Solve for a decay time
scenario: A sensor reading follows R = 80e^(−0.15t), with t in hours.

parts.prompt: Find the time when R first reaches 20, in hours.
parts.hint: Isolate the exponential before applying ln.

parts.prompt: Find the time for the reading to halve, in hours.
parts.hint: Set the ratio R/80 to 1/2.

reason: Explain why the time from 40 to 20 equals the time from 80 to 40.
discussion: An exponential model has a constant proportional decay factor; both transitions multiply the reading by 1/2, so they take the same time.

title: Bounds for a calculated density
scenario: A block has mass 84 g, rounded to the nearest gram, and volume 12.0 cm³, rounded to the nearest 0.1 cm³. Density is mass divided by volume.

parts.prompt: Find the infimum of the possible density, in g cm⁻³.
parts.hint: Use the smallest numerator and largest limiting denominator.

parts.prompt: Find the supremum of the possible density, in g cm⁻³.
parts.hint: Reverse the choices for the upper limit.

reason: Explain why these limiting density values are not attained under the usual half-open rounding intervals.
discussion: 83.5≤m<84.5 and 11.95≤V<12.05. The lower density requires excluded V=12.05; the upper requires excluded m=84.5. Therefore density lies strictly between the two limits.

title: A loan with a final smaller payment
scenario: Borrow 10000 at 6% nominal annual interest compounded monthly. Pay 300 at each month-end after interest. No fees.

parts.prompt: Find the balance just after payment 12.
parts.hint: Subtract the accumulated value of the payments.

parts.prompt: Find the smaller final payment at month 37, after 36 full payments.
parts.hint: Find B₃₆, then add one month of interest.
parts.working: Final payment = 1.005B₃₆ ≈ 166.80. It is less than the regular 300.

reason: Why does allowing a negative balance after a full final payment misrepresent the loan?
discussion: Once principal and accrued interest are cleared, no further debt remains. The final payment must be reduced to the outstanding amount rather than producing a fictitious credit balance.

title: Fit a quadratic from constraints
scenario: A quadratic y=ax²+bx+c passes through (0,3), (1,0) and (3,0).

parts.prompt: Find coefficient a.
parts.hint: Substitute each point to obtain three equations.
parts.working: c=3; a+b=−3; 9a+3b=−3. Subtracting 3a+3b=−9 gives 6a=6, so a=1.

parts.prompt: Find the smaller solution of y=8.
parts.hint: First find b, then solve the resulting quadratic.
parts.working: b=−4; x²−4x+3=8 gives x²−4x−5=0, with roots −1 and 5.

reason: Check both intersections and explain why solving only from a narrow graph window can miss one.
discussion: At x=−1 and 5, y=8. A window restricted to x≥0 would omit the negative intersection, although it remains a valid algebraic solution.

title: Two tariffs and a perpendicular
scenario: Tariff A costs y=3x+12. Tariff B passes through (2,24) and (6,40), where x is hours and y is cost.

parts.prompt: Find the algebraic x-coordinate of the intersection, even if outside the physical domain.
parts.hint: Find B’s slope and intercept, then equate the two lines.
parts.working: B has slope 4 and intercept 16. 3x+12=4x+16 gives x=−4. No equal cost occurs at non-negative hours.

parts.prompt: Find the slope of a line perpendicular to tariff B.
parts.hint: Use the negative reciprocal of B’s nonzero slope.

reason: Which tariff is cheaper for x≥0? Justify using the difference, not only a sketch.
discussion: B−A = x+4 > 0 for x≥0, so A is always cheaper in the physical domain. The algebraic intersection lies outside it.

title: Invert a restricted model
scenario: A pricing model is f(x)=5−2x on −1≤x≤3.

parts.prompt: Find the minimum value in the range.
parts.hint: The slope is negative; inspect the right endpoint.
parts.working: f(3)=−1 and f(−1)=7, so the range is [−1,7].

parts.prompt: Find f⁻¹(6).
parts.hint: Solve 6=5−2x, or use x=(5−y)/2.

reason: State the domain of the inverse and explain why f⁻¹(8) is not allowed here.
discussion: The inverse domain is [−1,7], the original range. Although the rearranged expression can take 8, that value was never an output of the restricted original function.

title: Combine a revenue and cost graph
scenario: Revenue R(x)=−x²+12x and cost C(x)=2x+9, for 0≤x≤10. Profit is R−C.

parts.prompt: Find the maximum profit.
parts.hint: Complete the square in −x²+10x−9.

parts.prompt: Find the larger break-even value of x.
parts.hint: Set the profit to zero.

reason: Identify where the business makes a loss in the stated domain.
discussion: Profit is positive between the roots, zero at 1 and 9, and negative for 0≤x<1 and 9<x≤10. Subtract graph heights in the correct order.

title: Choose a graph window
scenario: Consider f(x)=6/(x−2)+1.

parts.prompt: Find the x-intercept.
parts.hint: Set the whole function to zero and solve.

parts.prompt: Find the x-coordinate where f(x)=4.
parts.hint: Isolate the reciprocal term.

reason: State both asymptotes and explain why a vertical line drawn between plotted points either side of x=2 is misleading.
discussion: The asymptotes are x=2 and y=1. x=2 is outside the domain; joining samples across it draws a false part of the curve.

title: Fit a seasonal model
scenario: A seasonal quantity has maximum 18 and minimum 6. Its period is 12 months and a maximum occurs at t=0. Use y=a cos(bt)+d with degrees.

parts.prompt: Find a.
parts.hint: Amplitude is half the max–min difference.
parts.working: a=(18−6)/2=6; the principal axis is d=12.

parts.prompt: Find b in degrees per month.
parts.hint: Use period = 360/b.

reason: Predict y at t=3 and explain why the model should not automatically be extrapolated over decades.
discussion: At t=3, cos90°=0, so y=12. Long-term changes can alter the mean, amplitude or period; a periodic fit does not establish permanent repetition.

title: Validate a model
scenario: Fit y=ax²+bx+c through (0,2), (1,5), (2,12). A reserved observation at x=3 has y=22.

parts.prompt: Find a.
parts.hint: Use c=2, then solve a+b=3 and 4a+2b=10.
parts.working: Subtract twice the first equation: 2a=4, so a=2 and b=1.

parts.prompt: Find the reserved observation’s residual, observed minus predicted.
parts.hint: Predict at x=3 without refitting.

reason: Why is the reserved observation useful even when all three fitting points are matched exactly?
discussion: An exact fit to training points is guaranteed by the three-parameter construction. A separate observation tests prediction and can reveal a poor model family or measurement variation.

title: A composite container
scenario: A cylinder of radius 3 cm and height 8 cm is capped by a hemisphere of the same radius. Include the flat circular bottom but not the internal shared face.

parts.prompt: Find total volume in cm³.
parts.hint: Add cylinder volume and half a sphere.

parts.prompt: Find total external surface area in cm².
parts.hint: Add curved cylinder, curved hemisphere and bottom disk.

reason: If every length is doubled, by what factors do area and volume change? Explain dimensionally.
discussion: Area scales by 2²=4 and volume by 2³=8. The shared internal circular face is still excluded; doubling does not change which surfaces are external.

title: Resolve an ambiguous triangle
scenario: In triangle ABC, a=7, b=10 and angle A=30°. Lower-case sides are opposite matching angles.

parts.prompt: Find the smaller possible angle B in degrees.
parts.hint: Use sin B / b = sin A / a.

parts.prompt: Find the larger possible angle B in degrees.
parts.hint: Sine has the same value at B and 180°−B.
parts.working: The other B≈134.415°. Both leave positive angle C.

reason: Explain how to check whether both possibilities actually define triangles.
discussion: Compute C=180°−A−B in each case. Here C≈104.415° or 15.5847°, both positive; if one were zero or negative that candidate would be rejected.

title: Combine two journeys
scenario: A boat travels 12 km on bearing 030°, then 8 km on bearing 120°. Bearings are clockwise from north.

parts.prompt: Find its final east displacement in km.
parts.hint: East components use distance × sin(bearing).

parts.prompt: Find the direct distance from the starting point in km.
parts.hint: Sum north components too, then use Pythagoras.

reason: Explain why adding the travelled distances does not give displacement magnitude.
discussion: The 20 km total measures the route length. Displacement is the straight vector from start to finish; the direction changes between legs.

title: An annular sector
scenario: A sector-shaped strip has outer radius 10 cm, inner radius 6 cm and angle 72°.

parts.prompt: Find its area in cm².
parts.hint: Subtract two sector areas with the same angle.

parts.prompt: Find its full perimeter in cm.
parts.hint: Include both arcs and the two radial segments.
parts.working: Outer plus inner arcs = (72/360)2π(10+6)=6.4π; radial sides total 2(10−6)=8.

reason: Explain the common error of adding two complete radii to the arc lengths.
discussion: Only the strip is bounded: each straight side runs from radius 6 to radius 10 and has length 4, not 10.

title: A boundary between sites
scenario: A=(1,2), B=(7,6). Their perpendicular bisector has equation y=mx+c.

parts.prompt: Find m.
parts.hint: Find AB’s slope and use its negative reciprocal.

parts.prompt: Find c.
parts.hint: Use midpoint (4,4).

reason: Verify that (2,7) lies on the boundary by comparing squared distances.
discussion: It satisfies y=−1.5x+10. Squared distances to A and B are 1²+5²=26 and (−5)²+1²=26; equal distances confirm the boundary.

title: A three-site Voronoi vertex
scenario: Sites are A=(2,2), B=(8,2), C=(5,8), inside a square 0≤x,y≤10.

parts.prompt: Find the y-coordinate of the triple vertex.
parts.hint: A–B boundary is x=5; equate squared distances to A and C.

parts.prompt: Find the distance from that vertex to any site.
parts.hint: Use the distance to C, directly above the vertex.

reason: Is the triple vertex necessarily the point furthest from any site in this bounded map?
discussion: No. Compare all relevant Voronoi vertices and map-boundary candidates. For example corner (0,10) is √29≈5.385 from its nearest site C, larger than 3.75.

title: A biased sample with correct totals
scenario: A population has 600 commuters and 400 non-commuters. A sample of 80 should be proportionally stratified. A researcher instead takes volunteers within each quota.

parts.prompt: Find the commuter allocation.
parts.hint: Apply 600/1000 to the sample size.

parts.prompt: Find the non-commuter allocation.

reason: Explain why correct group totals alone do not make the volunteer sample stratified random sampling.
discussion: Within each stratum, selection must be random. Volunteers can differ systematically in interest, availability or travel habits, so quota proportions do not eliminate selection bias.

title: Estimate a grouped percentile
scenario: Equal-width intervals [0,10), [10,20), [20,30), [30,40) have frequencies 6,14,16,4. Use linear interpolation within classes.

parts.prompt: Estimate the median.
parts.hint: Locate cumulative position 0.5×40.
parts.working: Cumulative counts are 6,20,36,40. Position 20 is at the boundary 20.

parts.prompt: Estimate the 85th percentile.
parts.hint: Locate cumulative position 0.85×40 and interpolate within its class.
parts.working: Position 34 lies in [20,30), where cumulative frequency rises from 20 to 36. Estimate = 20 + (34−20)×10/16 = 28.75.

reason: Can these grouped data identify individual outliers exactly?
discussion: No. Class frequencies lose individual values. A cumulative graph provides estimated percentiles, but exact quartiles and individual outlier labels require the raw observations and a stated quartile convention.

title: Transform a weighted mean
scenario: Group A has 8 observations with mean 12. Group B has 12 observations with mean 17. The combined population SD is 4. Transform every value by y=3x−5.

parts.prompt: Find the combined original mean.
parts.hint: Combine sums, not the two unweighted means.

parts.prompt: Find the transformed population variance.
parts.hint: SD is multiplied by 3; variance by 9.

reason: Find the transformed mean and explain why subtracting 5 does not reduce the SD by 5.
discussion: New mean=3×15−5=40. Translation moves all values and their mean equally, leaving distances from the mean unchanged.

title: Residuals and extrapolation
scenario: A regression model is y=1.8x+4, fitted using x-values from 2 to 8. At x=5 the observation is y=11.

parts.prompt: Find that observation’s residual.
parts.hint: Use observed minus fitted.

parts.prompt: Find the model prediction at x=12.
parts.hint: Substitute 12 into the fitted line.

reason: Explain why the second answer deserves more caution, even if the original correlation is strong.
discussion: x=12 lies outside the observed range, so this is extrapolation. A strong association over 2≤x≤8 does not show that the same linear trend continues to 12 or establishes causation.

title: Use a complement carefully
scenario: Two fair six-sided dice are rolled. Ordered pairs are equally likely.

parts.prompt: Find the probability that at least one die shows 6.
parts.hint: Complement: neither die is 6.

parts.prompt: Find the expected count of this event in 720 independent rolls of both dice.
parts.hint: Multiply number of experiments by the event probability.

reason: Why is adding 1/6 and 1/6 incorrect here?
discussion: The outcome (6,6) is counted twice. Subtract the overlap 1/36, or use the complement. Expected count is not a guaranteed actual count.

title: A diagnostic probability
scenario: A fictional test has positive probability 0.9 for affected people and 0.1 for unaffected people. Prevalence is 0.02.

parts.prompt: Find the overall probability of a positive result.
parts.hint: Split into affected and unaffected branches.

parts.prompt: Find P(affected | positive).
parts.hint: Divide the affected-and-positive probability by all positives.

reason: Explain why 90% sensitivity does not mean a positive result has 90% probability of indicating an affected person.
discussion: Sensitivity conditions on affected status; the question conditions on a positive result. At low prevalence, many positives come from the much larger unaffected group. This is a fictional probability model, not medical advice.

title: Set a fair game fee
scenario: A prize X takes values 0,5,20 with probabilities 0.6,0.3,0.1. A player pays fee f.

parts.prompt: Find the fair fee.
parts.hint: Set expected net gain E(X−f) to zero.

parts.prompt: At fee 4, find the expected total net gain over 200 plays.
parts.hint: Use linearity of expectation.

reason: Does a fair fee imply every player breaks even after a short session?
discussion: No. Fairness concerns expected value over repeated play. Actual prizes fluctuate and individual results can be far from their expectation.

title: A binomial threshold
scenario: X is the number of successes in 8 independent trials, each with success probability 0.25.

parts.prompt: Find P(X≥2).
parts.hint: Subtract probabilities of zero and one success from 1.

parts.prompt: Find Var(X).
parts.hint: Use np(1−p).

reason: Explain why sampling 8 items without replacement from a small finite batch can invalidate this binomial model.
discussion: The probability of success changes as items are removed and outcomes become dependent. A binomial model requires constant p and independent trials.

title: Recover a normal model
scenario: A normal variable has 10th percentile 42 and 90th percentile 58. Use z₀.₉=1.2815515655.

parts.prompt: Find the mean.
parts.hint: The percentiles are symmetric about the mean.

parts.prompt: Find the standard deviation.
parts.hint: The distance from mean to the 90th percentile is zσ.

reason: Why does this pair of percentiles not prove the data follow a normal distribution?
discussion: Other distributions can share these percentiles. The calculation assumes normality; assess shape, tails and context before accepting that model.

title: Tied ranks and an extreme value
scenario: x=(1,2,3,4,5), y=(10,20,20,40,100). Assign increasing averaged ranks.

parts.prompt: Find the rank assigned to each y=20.
parts.hint: Average occupied positions 2 and 3.

parts.prompt: Find Spearman’s rank correlation.
parts.hint: Compute Pearson correlation of x-ranks and y-ranks.
parts.working: Ranks are (1,2,3,4,5) and (1,2.5,2.5,4,5). Cross-deviation sum=9.5; squared sums=10 and 9.5; rₛ=9.5/√95≈0.974679.

reason: What happens to Spearman’s coefficient if 100 is replaced by 1000? Contrast with Pearson on the original values.
discussion: The ranks do not change, so Spearman stays the same. Pearson uses numerical distances and can change substantially. Avoid the no-ties shortcut formula when ties exist.

title: A goodness-of-fit decision
scenario: A fair three-category spinner predicts equal proportions. In 60 trials the observed counts are 30,20,10. For df=2, upper-tail p=exp(−χ²/2).

parts.prompt: Find the chi-square statistic.
parts.hint: Expected counts are 20 each; sum (O−E)²/E.

parts.prompt: Find the p-value.
parts.hint: Use the supplied df=2 survival formula.

reason: State decisions at 5% and 1%, and explain what rejecting H₀ does not show.
discussion: Reject equal probabilities at both levels because p<0.01. This does not prove a particular alternative distribution or give P(H₀ true). Independent trials and adequate expected counts are required; all E=20>5.

title: From a secant to an instantaneous rate
scenario: Distance is s(t)=t²+3t metres. Compare rates at t=2 seconds.

parts.prompt: Find the average rate from t=2 to t=2.5, in m/s.
Find the instantaneous rate at t=2, in m/s.
parts.hint: Differentiate or take the limit of the secant expression.

reason: Derive the average rate over [2,2+h] and use it to justify the limit.
discussion: The quotient is [(2+h)²+3(2+h)−10]/h = 7+h for h≠0. As h approaches zero, this approaches 7.

title: Interpret derivative signs
scenario: f(x)=x³−6x²+9x+2 on 0≤x≤5.

parts.prompt: Find the smaller stationary x-value.
parts.hint: Factor f′(x)=3x²−12x+9.
parts.working: f′=3(x−1)(x−3), so the smaller root is 1.

parts.prompt: Find the length of the interval where f is decreasing.
parts.hint: The derivative is negative between its roots.
parts.working: Decreasing for 1<x<3, an interval of length 2.

reason: Explain why f can be positive while f′ is negative.
discussion: The value measures height; the derivative measures change. For example f(2)=4>0 but f′(2)=−3<0: the graph is above the axis while falling.

title: Differentiate negative powers
scenario: f(x)=2x³+6x⁻²−4 for x>0.

parts.prompt: Find f′(2).
parts.hint: Differentiate each power, including the negative exponent.

parts.prompt: Find the positive x-value where f′(x)=0.
parts.hint: Multiply the derivative equation by x³.

reason: Why is multiplying by x³ safe here, and what domain restriction must be retained?
discussion: The original function excludes zero and is restricted to x>0. Thus x³ is nonzero, so multiplying preserves solutions within that domain; do not introduce x=0.

title: Intersect a normal with an axis
scenario: For y=x²−2x, find the normal at x=3.

parts.prompt: Find the normal slope.
parts.hint: Tangent slope is 2x−2.
parts.working: At x=3 tangent slope=4, so normal slope=−1/4.

parts.prompt: Find the x-intercept of that normal.
parts.hint: The point is (3,3); set y=0 in y−3=−(x−3)/4.

reason: Why is taking the reciprocal without changing sign incorrect?
discussion: Nonvertical perpendicular lines have slope product −1. A positive reciprocal would give product +1 and would not form a right angle.

title: Recover a function and an area
scenario: F′(x)=3x²−4x+5 and F(1)=7. The integrand 3x²−4x+5 is positive.

parts.prompt: Find C in F(x)=x³−2x²+5x+C.
parts.hint: Apply the boundary value at x=1.

parts.prompt: Find the integral of 3x²−4x+5 from 1 to 3.
parts.hint: Evaluate the antiderivative at both limits.

reason: Explain why the constant affects the boundary condition but not the definite integral.
discussion: The boundary condition fixes a particular antiderivative. In F(3)−F(1), the same C is subtracted from itself, so it cancels.

title: Local versus global extrema
scenario: f(x)=x³−3x on −2≤x≤3.

parts.prompt: Find the local minimum value.
parts.hint: Use derivative sign changes at x=±1.
parts.working: At x=1 derivative changes negative to positive; f(1)=−2.

parts.prompt: Find the global maximum value on this closed interval.
parts.hint: Check endpoints as well as stationary points.
parts.working: Values: f(−2)=−2, f(−1)=2, f(1)=−2, f(3)=18. Global maximum=18.

reason: Why is the local maximum at x=−1 not the global maximum?
discussion: It is greater than nearby values but not all values in the domain. The endpoint at x=3 has a much larger value; closed-interval optimization must inspect endpoints.

title: Optimize an open box
scenario: Cut equal squares of side x cm from the corners of a 20 cm by 12 cm sheet, then fold an open box. Use 0<x<6.

parts.prompt: Find x giving maximum volume, in cm.
parts.hint: V=x(20−2x)(12−2x); solve V′=0 and keep roots in the domain.

parts.prompt: Find the maximum volume in cm³.
parts.hint: Substitute the unrounded x into the volume expression.
parts.working: V≈262.682 cm³. The other stationary root is outside the physical domain.

reason: Justify a maximum using the derivative and boundary behaviour.
discussion: V′ changes positive to negative at the allowed root. Volume tends to zero at both ends of (0,6), so this stationary point gives the global physical maximum.

title: A trapezoidal estimate from measurements
scenario: A flow rate in L/min is recorded at times 0,2,4,6 minutes as 1,3,4,2 respectively.

parts.prompt: Estimate total volume in litres using the trapezoidal rule.
parts.hint: Strip width is 2 minutes.

parts.prompt: A flow meter reports an exact total of 16 L. Find the percentage error of the estimate.
parts.hint: Use |estimate−reference|/reference ×100.

reason: Can these four observations alone establish whether the trapezoidal rule overestimates the unknown curve?
discussion: No. The curve between measurements is unknown. It could bend above or below the chords; the reference total reveals the direction in this instance, not the samples alone.
